compared.difference: The only public item of this article counts the omega-squared example T(2, omega^2) = 4, whose upper and lower bounds use the coefficient and colouring-rule machinery for ordinals below omega^omega. This target is about the ordered set of integers, which is not an ordinal and is not order-equivalent to omega^2, and its proof is the article's separate direct argument with a sign-alternating reconstruction; neither statement implies the other and no step is shared.

That card counts the exact big Ramsey degree of finite powers omega^d through canonical coefficient patterns and the finite pattern count. This target counts a degree for the integers, where no coefficient pattern exists, so the counting objects and the proofs are disjoint.

That card counts the general equality for every ordinal alpha below omega^omega, with the mixed-exponent block construction and the generalized colouring rules. The integers are not an ordinal at all, so T(2,zeta) lies outside its scope; the article itself announces the integers result in a separate section and proves it without the ordinal machinery.

compared.difference: The general integers theorem of the same article, T(n,zeta) = 2^n at source lines 553-591, is deliberately NOT counted: its printed lower bound ends by leaving the absence of a zeta-(2^n - 1)-homogeneous set to the reader at source lines 588-589, so the article's printed proof is incomplete there. The n = 1 sibling T(1,zeta) = 2 at source lines 473-493 has its own complete proof but is the same integers counting object with one element and is subsumed by the general theorem, so it is not counted either; the counted n = 2 theorem is the one case that carries a complete printed proof of both bounds.
